The Short Answer: What Is a Euploid Embryo?

It is an embryo whose tested cells show exactly 46 chromosomes, with no extra or missing copies. The word comes from Greek: "eu" means good or normal, and "ploid" refers to sets of chromosomes. The opposite is an aneuploid embryo, which has too many or too few chromosomes and usually cannot lead to a healthy pregnancy.
So the euploid embryo meaning is simple: as far as the test can tell, the embryo's chromosome count is normal. You learn this from

, where an embryologist removes a few cells from the outer layer of a day 5 to 7 blastocyst and sends them for analysis. At Aurea Fertility Center, PGT costs $950 per embryo, and the embryo is frozen while you wait for results.

A euploid result tells you about chromosome number only. It does not test every gene, and it does not test your uterus, your lining or the timing of your transfer. That is why a normal result raises your odds but cannot promise a pregnancy.
Euploid, aneuploid and mosaic at a glance
normal chromosome count. Usually first in line for transfer.
an extra or missing chromosome. Usually not transferred.
a mix of normal and abnormal cells in the sample. Some mosaic embryos can still lead to healthy births, and the choice is made with your doctor and a genetic counselor.
When a Euploid Embryo Gives You the Best Odds
The odds are strongest when you are under 38, your uterus is healthy, and the embryo has good quality. In that setting, about half to more than half of single euploid transfers lead to a live birth.
2025 study in the Journal of Ovarian Research

followed 1,037 single euploid embryo transfers. The live birth rate was 54.5% for women under 35 and 54.0% for women aged 35 to 37. That is a strong number, and it is one reason many people choose a single embryo transfer instead of two embryos at once, which avoids the risks of twins.

What the Research Shows About Euploid Embryo Success Rates
The research shows that a euploid embryo success rate is high but not 100%, that age still matters a little after testing, and that embryo grade and day matter less than many people expect.

(Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics, 2020), women 38 and older had lower implantation than women under 35, with odds ratios of 0.85 at 38 to 40 and 0.69 above 40. The authors concluded that factors other than chromosomes contribute to age-related decline.
2025 study of 538 single euploid frozen transfers

in Reproductive Sciences found that only the trophectoderm grade made a difference: grade A outer cells had a higher live birth rate than grade C. Expansion and inner cell mass grade did not change the live birth rate.
In that same study, euploid embryos that formed on day 5, 6 or 7 had similar live birth rates. Across all blastocysts, tested or not, a
found higher live birth after day 5 transfer (risk ratio 1.50), so day 5 euploid embryos are usually transferred first when you have a choice.
The test is accurate, not perfect.

Why Does a Euploid Embryo Transfer Fail?

A transfer can fail because chromosomes are only one part of implantation. The embryo still has to attach to a receptive lining at the right time, and the test itself has small limits. Women in fertility forums ask this again and again, often after a loss that felt impossible: "Was it fifth time lucky for anyone?"
Here are the main reasons, in plain terms:
The embryo had a problem the test could not see.
PGT-A counts chromosomes from a few outer cells. It does not check every gene, and the inner cell mass can occasionally differ from the sample.
Polyps, fibroids, scarring, a thin lining or fluid from a blocked tube can all block implantation.
The lining has a window when it accepts an embryo, and progesterone timing in an FET cycle matters.
Research on 8,175 transfers suggests egg health and other factors still play a role after 38.
Even under ideal conditions, about half of single euploid transfers do not lead to a birth. One failed transfer does not mean the next will fail.

That last point matters. Many people do go on to succeed. One woman wrote, "I am pregnant from my fourth Euploid and fifth transfer." Another reminded a worried poster that "there's still a good chance it could work!"
What the 2026 ASRM guidance says to check, and what to skip
2026 ASRM committee opinion on recurrent implantation failure

defines recurrent implantation failure after 3 to 6 failed euploid transfers. It recommends repeating the uterine and tubal assessment, by saline sonogram, hysteroscopy, HSG or 3D ultrasound, and says hysteroscopy can treat problems found at the same visit.
It also lists tests and treatments that are

routinely for recurrent implantation failure, because they have not been shown to improve live birth: endometrial receptivity testing (ERA), immune therapies including IVIG, endometrial scratching and routine sperm DNA fragmentation testing. Knowing this can save you money and time. If you have had recurrent losses or several failed transfers, our
team can talk through which evaluations make sense for you.

What is the success rate of a euploid embryo transfer?

In a 2025 study of 1,037 single euploid transfers, live birth rates were 54.5% under 35, 54.0% at 35 to 37 and 41.7% at 38 and older. Rates vary by clinic, embryo grade and uterine health, so ask your clinic for its own figures.
What does euploid embryo meaning on my report tell me?

It means the cells tested from your embryo showed the normal 46 chromosomes, with no extra or missing copies. It does not test every gene or your uterus. It tells you the embryo has the best chromosome profile for implantation.
Does embryo grade matter if the embryo is euploid?

A little. A 2025 study found that trophectoderm grade A embryos had higher live birth rates than grade C, while expansion and inner cell mass grade did not change outcomes. Your embryologist will usually transfer the best-graded euploid embryo first.
Can a euploid embryo result in miscarriage?
Yes. In the 2025 study, miscarriage after euploid transfer was 13.0% under 35 and 12.8% at 35 to 37. A loss after a euploid transfer is a reason to check the uterus and review your plan.
How many euploid embryo transfers should I try before more testing?

The 2026 ASRM committee opinion defines recurrent implantation failure after 3 to 6 failed euploid transfers. Many doctors review the uterus after the first failure. A full work-up after 3 failed euploid transfers is a reasonable plan to discuss.
Is a day 6 euploid embryo as good as a day 5?

In a 2025 study of euploid frozen transfers, day 5, 6 and 7 euploid embryos had similar live birth rates. Across all blastocysts, day 5 transfers do slightly better, so the day 5 embryo usually goes first when you have both.
A chromosomally normal embryo is the strongest one you can transfer, and under 38 about half of single euploid transfers lead to a baby.
Euploid means better odds, not a guarantee, and a failed transfer is a reason to review the plan, not a verdict on your future.
